blocks.x: PROCEEDINGS

Helen and Stanley Dance are interviewing Freddie Green
August 9, 1977.
Freddie, we want to ask you where and when you were born and we want you to digress at length about your background. So, when were you?
I was born on March 31, 1911, in Charleston, South Carolina. It's a place on Rutledge Avenue.
Rutledge?
Rutledge.
Yeah.
And there's a court there called Dafts Court. It's -- about twelve houses.
How do you spell Dafts?
D-A-L-T-S. And, there's twelve houses on it, and I was born in one of them -- number 7, Dafts Court.
Yeah, number 7, Dafts Court. That was maybe -- kind of nice -- to be in a court rather than on the street?
Yeah -- it's a court with twelve -- right off of Rutledge Avenue.
Now Charleston is very pretty isn't it? We drove into it this year and it's very pretty.
Yes, it's a beautiful place -- a beautiful city.
So was it nice, shady trees and everything?
Well, they had trees, -- yes.
Yeah.
There's alot of trees around there.
Yeah. Where is Rutledge? Does it run right through the center of town or where does it run?
Yes. It runs right through the center of town. It's one of the main streets there in Charleston, and this is right between -- there's two streets in between, which is Race and Rutledge --
Yeah.
Race and something-or-other -- along Rutledge.
I see.
And right in the middle is this court called DaIts Court.
That's nice. How long had the family lived there?
Well, let's see. I lived there until 1923, and then came to New York.
You did?
Yes.
So the whole first part of your life you lived there?
Yes.
That's nice. How many in the family?
Just me and a couple of brothers --
Is that right?
-- Clarence and Josey.
Older?
No, they were younger.
They were younger?
Yeah. They were born you know there -- Clarence was there, who was born at a different time than I was, and I left and I went to New York. Then my mother got married and had my other brother.
Yeah. So he was quite a bit younger than you?
Yes.
Well, why don't we just talk about that. Where are they now?
Well, one of them is in Charleston.
Which one?
Joe.
And what does he do?
He's working for the Armed Services more or less, at the Navy Yard there.
Oh
He's a cook.
Do you see him when you go through?
Oh, I usually go around and see him.
You do? He's got family I guess?
Yes.
Yeah
Yeah.
Was he musical?
No, not really.
Was Clarence?
No.
Well, who was musical? Your mother?
My father used to play the organ more or less.
Did he?
Yeah.
Weren't organs hard to get your hands on in those days?
Oh, DANCE: one of those harmoniums, Yeah, one of those use Well, it was one of those things that you -- with your foot.
Did he have it in the house, you mean?
Yeah, Yes, it was in the house. In other words it was in my Aunt's house.
Oh, was that also in Dalts Court?
Yes.
Oh, That was nice. they lived what, They lived next door or what?
We lived in (number) seven and they were in ten -- right across the way from us.
That was nice. Was that his sister? Or your mother's sister?
No, Yes, My father's sister.
Your father's sister. Was she musical?
No, no.
But your father was?
Yes.
What kind of things did he play?
Oh -- as I could its hard to remember. I was quite young.
Or was he, he wasn't playing He wasn't playing
I mean was it rhythmic? church music?
No. No, no. (laugh).
(laugh). Okay.
(laugh) It was, [stride] [ ]
(playfully) I don't know what's funny about that.
(Laugh)
Alright. So he was playing what -- well, let's see that was -- was this like you'd be 9 or 10?
No. Well, my father died when I was about -- I'd say maybe -- 10 or 11.
Did he really? How did he die?
Well, I don't know. you know at that age. I don't know what happened.
No, no. He just fell sick?
Its kind of hard to remember -- something like that.
But, so what memory you have of him playing was when you were 9 -- 8 or 9.
yes. Yes, something like that.
So, and I mean, that would have been in 1915, 17, or 18 or something like that.
Something like that.
So, maybe it was like ragtime or something he was playing.
It could have been, during that period.
Yeah. Was that exactly when it was ragtime then? time?
No, no -- you know, he could have been playing sort of popular songs of the day, you know.
Yeah -- he could have. I don't know what he played but --
Well, then --
I don't think it was church -- but I don't know what he played.
No
Its surprising how many sort of standard jazz songs go right back -- you know, you think of jazz starting around 1920, but alot of those standards were written 1914-15-16 --
What -- things like "Back in Your Own Back Yard" and things like that?
Yeah -- no, not that, but --
Well, no, no I don't know I think maybe a little no further back than that.
(unintelligible) You know, became more or less, um, making a part of the jazz world.
Whatever was happening during that period I imagine he was probably playing. I don't know
(softly) Yeah, that's what he was doing.
Do you think everything is coming through loud enough Stan -- your voice too?
Sure. Want me to check it? Okay.
Okay, that's fine. Well, Uh, Freddie then your mother
didn't marry again right then?
No, she married ...
So she had to bring you and Clarence up on her own?
Yes.
What did she do? How did she manage?
Well, she was --. Domestic work.
So that means that you were off at school and --
(Uh-huh)
-- I guess she wouldn't be home when you got home? Not always I suppose? What -- you'd get back from school -- four or five or something?
Yeah, -- about four o'clock or something like that --
And she wouldn't be home?
-- and she wouldn't be home. She'd be on her way home.
No. So what all mischief did you get into? (laugh)
(laugh). Well, I got into all kinds of mischief.
Well, tell us. Like what for instance?
Well, I don't remember them now -- I mean we were just normal kids you know --
No, I know, I mean -- did you have good buddies that lived right there in the court.
Oh yeah. You know, there's alot of families there --
Yeah?
-- in the court, so -- we got along. Plus friends that, you know --
Yeah?
-- were ours. We'd play, and go out in town. Walking out in town selling papers -- shining shoes.
Oh you would?
Yes.
Oh, you would?
You know, to make a little money.
To make some -- a little money?
Yes.
Yeah.
How big a city would it have been in those days -- I mean -- its expanded alot since then --
Yes. Yes it has, but how big during that period -- I wouldn't know.
But what was it -- what was --. I remember Trummy Young saying that -- you know he'd been brought up in Savannah and he said that life there was really not too bad --
(mm hmm)
-- as compared with the South generally.
(mm hmm)
You know because it was a port I guess.
Mm hmm. Mm hmm.
Well how did -- I mean -- you find it in those days. Although I guess you were too young to sort of --
(Ummmm) No -- I was -- it was -- there was bad times and there were good times there --
Yeah.
-- in Charleston. I mean we had we had the racial problem you know and -- but --
Yeah.
And poverty?
Right -- and poverty. So -- but we got along --
(pause).
And made your own fun?
Yeah. Yeah.
Well, and you were saying -- you knew the sort of conditions and knew what to do.
Yeah. You know what to do and you - you know -- act accordingly, and -- that's about it.
Well, listen Freddie -- how old were you when you left? Did you say?
I came to New York when I was --
You said 1923.
Yeah. 1923.
And you were born 1909?
I think I was what -- twelve or thirteen or something like that when I came -- to New York.
You left home at twelve or thirteen?
Yes.
Merciful heavens!
Yes.
By yourself?
Well, no. My Aunt see -- my mother's sister --
Yeah?
-- moved to New York.
Was she in Charleston?
Oh yeah. She had lived in Charleston. Then she moved to New York. But she was in New York, if I can remember, say two or three years or something like that.
Yeah?
And then my mother -- it was just my mother --
She moved to New York?
Yes. She moved in the Sixties.
Oh yes.
Right. Early Sixties. And uh...
Right, right. Do you know where Freddie means Stanley?
Yeah. That was where Benny Carter was.
Right, Benny Carter lived right on 163rd.
Right. That's right. And a whole lot of Irish people lived there.
Yeah, yeah, right.
And um, after that she moved to New York, then I came -- my mother sent me on to New York,
Yeah.
How did she send you up -- on the train?
Yes.
Alone?
No, I came with my Aunt -- which is --
She came down to visit or came down to get you?
No, My uncle, who is my mother's brother --
Yeah--
-- his wife --
Yeah --
-- left Charleston and went to New York --
Yeah --
-- to my Aunt who was already in New York.
I see.
And then I went rode with her on the train.
I see. Well, that's what I wanted to know -- when you went. So really, in a sense, your memories and everything of Charleston -- they're not very full really because they ended at thirteen.
No. Right.
How much visiting did you ever do after that?
Oh, I came back --
Regularly?
Periodically. Not too often.
To stay with family or --
But, that's afterwards.
Yeah. After you had gone up?
Yeah. After I had gone up and I went to school and everything in New York.
Yeah, I see.
And then I went back because my mother died.
Oh. How old were you when your mother died.
I was nineteen -- eighteen, nineteen.
How did she die -- do you know?
No.
No
Eighteen or nineteen.
But you were with her -- before she died?
No, I wasn't there.
Oh.
No.
In other words, Because I couldn't get back.
Yeah.
You know.
Yeah. You didn't know in time or you couldn't reach them?
And then I came back to New York, uh, to bury her, in other words. And I stayed down.
Well?
Then I got married after that
Down there?
Down there.
Oh, you did. Well, alright -- we're going too fast.
Yeah. Oh.
Well, so let's get back, really, to where you're still a kid, because you know, this -- like they say --what do they say? The "child is father to the man"-- or whatever it is they say.
Mm hmm.
You know -- really you come out how you are -- as a kid.
Mm hmm.
You know -- really I think, whatever happened. Don't you?
Duke always showed how he really was when he was young.
Well, I mean like, were you a leader amongst the kids? Or were you a part of a gang or were you on the side of the gang, or how did it work?
No, I was a part of the gang.
A part --
I was with the group more or less. You know, everything we did, we did together.
Yeah? And did you play ball and?
Oh yeah, yeah. I played ball and most of the sports.
Oh you did?
Yeah.
Yeah.
And -- (pause).
Were you tall or not so tall.
I was skinny.
Oh. You were skinny?
Yeah,
(Laugh)
(Laugh) I was a skinny kid (pause) in those days.
When do you get interested though in music?
Well, I used -- before I left -- I used to -- I think after I came back -- after I came back to -- say -- buried my brother and my mother more or less -- Well, my mother was in the church.
Oh, she was? Yeah?
Right. Okay?
A Holiness Church?
Huh?
A Holiness Church or a Baptist Church?
A Methodist Church. AME.
AME?
AME Church. And, she used to sing alot. She sang in the choir, and I used to sing along with her at home, you know.
Did she have a pretty voice?
Oh Yeah. And, then I used to play the ukelele.
Oh you did?
Yeah.
When you were still a kid?
Yeah.
She bought you one?
I don't remember how I got it (laugh). I really don't.
Somebody maybe had one and you --
Yeah. Yeah.
Well, ukeleles were real popular weren't they?
Yes. Yeah. I don't remember. I don't remember.
Yeah. But you did?
Yeah.
And you used to sing? Sing along?
Yeah. And then they used to sing on corners like quartets, you know what I mean. We used to get together --
Yeah?
-- and sing on corners. And I used to sing Irish songs. It was four voices in other words, and I used to be more or less the baritone singer I sang baritone.
Oh, you did?
Like a barbershop harmony thing.
Yeah. With a harmony -- the barbershop.
Yeah. Right.
And you'd pick up some nickels and dimes?
Yeah!
What would you do -- hold out a hat or?
No, no. We didn't go in for that. And I was the youngest in the group more or less, you know what I mean? And these guys were bigger than me.
Yeah.
But I had the voice that they needed so I --
Yeah?
Just at night, just for our own amusement. -- get out and just
Perform. You did? You'd just perform.
Yeah. You know. Just -- that's all.
Very nice.
Yeah.
Yeah.
It was very nice.
So that was your first taste of music, right?
Really.
Well, did you have a feel then for the beat, for something--?
Oh, well, I used to dance. I was a good dancer, more or less.
Oh, were you?
Cause my mother was a good dancer and I was always able to dance I used to.
You mean like some tap dancing? Would you, you know, do some tap dancing? Or some beats and steps?
Yeah. No, no. You know --
You just danced?
Yeah. Right. That's right.
To enjoy it. Do a little dance.
Yeah. But during that period -- later on that came--. I used to go to movies, oh, quite a bit. I loved the movies.
Yeah?
I used to live in the -- in the movies.
Yeah?
I remember when I was a kid my mother used to say when she looked for me I was always in the movies. (Laugh). That's where they had stage shows. And I loved stage shows during that period.
Yeah. Yeah.
And I remember once that Mamie Smith --
Oh? You do?
-- came to a theater there. And whenever they would have a stage show I would go.
Yeah.
Now we couldn't sit downstairs. We had to go upstairs.
Yeah.
So, I used to go up there and watch -- watch them dance. And then come home and like, imitate them. You know the dances and whatnot.
Yeah. Yeah. Well, who did you see in those days? Can you remember, I mean, do you --
No --
Guys like [Cock] and [Brown] or guys like --
Oh no, no.
I guess that was later, huh?
No, no. That's too early.
That was too early for stuff like that?
I'm talking about way back.
Yeah. Yeah.
You know, this is a long time ago.
Yeah, yeah.
You know, like I was a kid, you know.
Yeah.
And I imagine this was -- well they had the theaters there -- these different shows used to come through. I remember one show was -- came through there -- the Whitman Sisters.
Have you ever heard that?
Whitman?
Whitman. W-H-I-T-M-A-N.
Were they black or white?
They were black.
I've heard of sisters called the Whitman -- Whit-M-A-N. Whitman.
That's what Freddie said.
Yeah. Right.
Yeah, man, I know you must have heard about them. You must, as far as history is concerned.
Yeah.

They have got to be recorded somehow. But the Whitman sisters -- they came through, and they had two kids. Two kids used to dance with -- oh, what's the name of those kids? You see, remember we had a Pops and Louie. Have you ever heard of them, Pops --
Yeah.
A dance team called Pops and Louie. Now Pops -- he was the kid of the Whitman Sisters. They were -- the two sisters -- they were dancers. They were terrific tap dancers.
They were?
And they had -- they would -- little Pops -- he was the son.
And then?
And he was a kid during that period. And I used to go to this theater, and I saw them in Charleston, I was, you know. And, as I say I used to watch them dance and come back home --
Oh Get home and --
-- and try to imitate what they did.
Yeah.
And Mamie Smith --
Mamie -- Yeah, right.
-- and other blues singers, etcetera, came through there, too?
Yeah, all of the blues singers. But I remember her, you know, coming through there.
Well, what do you remember of her. Tell me more -- what how it was?
I mean, she wasn't as good as Bessie, was she?
No, no. Well, I don't know, whether really, you know. During that period, as I say, I was a kid, really, I don't know what --
Was she a big woman?
I don't know. I don't remember whether if she was big.
Yeah, you just don't remember the details --
Just vaguely, you know, I remember back that far.
And what would they do? Would they have --
They would have a group of a couple of instruments --
A couple of instruments? What instruments?
You know, like the piano, I think a drum and a trumpet -- are the ones I remember. I'm sure they must have had --

have struck you.
Mm hmm.
Do you remember anything like that? Maybe you actually never heard anything that really hit? down there Mr. Dance: I bet you did.
Not really. Well.

That's true.
Yeah. Well --
I don't know.
Another thing that I remember was [Jenkin's] Orphanage.
Oh.
[Jenkin's] Orphanage.
The group?
It was an orphanage. They had five or six bands, you know. Underprivileged kids, you know
Yeah.
And they all had instruments, and used to play. They used to go on corners and play on every other corner and play.
Well, you mean they were in Charleston, too?
Jenkin's Orphanage?
Yeah.
Heck, yeah.
Well, was there a Jenkin's Orphanage in alot of places?
No.
No.
No.
No, Charleston is--
That's where it was?
That's where it was. In the center, Charleston is the -- as far as music is concerned, I mean, Charleston has always been musical.
Really? And they had about five different bands?

And they had about five different bands. And they could -- because they used to send them all over the city, in other words, to work on different street corners and, you know, pick up money that way to help the orphanage.
The orphanage? And they had -- so they had those instruments --
They used to come on my neighborhood, and I used to stop whatever I was doing, and follow them all over the city.
No kidding.
Would they be sort of marching band sort of? of thing?
Marching band, you know. Yeah. They were a marching band. But they would play the 'St. Louis Blues' and all of the -- whatever was happening during that period.
Yeah.
You know -- the trombone -- they were strictly a brass band, more or less.
Yeah. Drums I guess, too?
They specialized in drums and the brass.
-- And the brass. Mr. Greene: Right. Did you ever know any -- was there anyone there blowing that you came to know afterwards?
Later on. Yes.
Who?
Oh, like Charlie Anderson --
Charlie Anderson was from the Jenkin's Orphanage? Mr. Dance: Yeah.
Yeah. There's so many -- listen, there are so many musicians who --

Like the guys before my time. I used to hear about a guy called Specs. And there's a guy -- about -- oh, so many different -- I can't think of it --
Trumpet players?
Trumpet players --

No. I heard about him.
Briscoe was supposed to be --
Yeah. I heard about him. I heard quite a bit about him.

No, no, no. Not that old. Maybe, I'd say from maybe seven to about fourteen or fifteen.
You mean that kids seven and eight would be out blowing their horns?

Heck, yeah. Yeah, they trained, you know, real young. And they were on the corner playing -- seven, you know -- say about from seven on up to about -- I'd say about fourteen or fifteen years old, or sixteen.

All over. Anywhere. Well, you see, Charleston was a city that -- there's no "across the track".
Oh, there isn't? Everything is everywhere.
You know, there's whites here, blacks here.
Everything is everywhere?
So there was no -- I mean there was no separation, not really.
No? No. Which is good, isn't it Freddie? It's better --
No, no. It was okay.
Yeah.
There's a few little things way back.
Yeah.
As far as the music end of it is concerned, Jenkin's was all over the city. You know, they would play -- and I would just follow them all over. Wherever they'd go. I think
that had alot to do with it. The minute I heard that brass, I --
(laugh) Any of the other kids you played with like you?
Oh yeah, you know, you know, how kids are, we'd get together and follow all over the place.
Yeah.

Right. Right.
I mean, you wouldn't get that at school would you?
No, no, no.
No.
Not during that period you didn't have anything like -- like, you know, bands in schools.
So they had quite alot of instruments if they could put five bands out.
Oh, yeah.
Well, then they sent the bands out through the country?

Fancy that.
Yeah.

Reverend Jenkins.
It was Reverend Jenkins?
Reverend Jenkins.
He must have been a -- good person.
Yeah, yeah.
It took alot of foresight.
Yeah.

Well, yeah. You know, after they get about sixt--
When they get through --
Yeah.
When they could get out of school.
Yeah. When they could get out. You know, they would go.
Fancy that. Do you remember their orphanage where they lived?
Yes.

Well, I mean, it would be partly like a reform school?
A reform -- yeah. A regular -- like a regular reform school. The kids couldn't -- they couldn't get out. It's not like they had them fenced in.
No.
I didn't get that impression.
No.
I don't think the kids really wanted to leave, anyway.
Yeah.
Or get away.
Yeah.

No.

They did?
Yeah.
I don't remember that, because, being on the outside, I don't know what happened on the inside.
They probably didn't need to, either.
I think, you know, he said they'd have to stand on this tree stump for hours, you know, without moving, and things like that, if they did anything wrong.
Oh yeah, how a lot of schools were,

Yeah, I imagine so.
Yeah.

Mm hmm.
-- and you would hear those bands -- the Jenkins' bands --

-- and you had yourself a ukelele --

Oh yeah. Very close.

Yeah. And I just, like, saw them all off, you know.

She was.

Huh?

Yeah. The lights and everything.
The lights, and what they were doing on stage, and how they did it. I used to just go and watch them, you know, attentively and watch.

Mm

-- where you stayed.

Yeah.
I don't know.

There's one thing I'd like to comment on in any of the bands which, of course, it is Basie -- basically is responsible for it -- isn't he? -- what is great. What puts a smile on your face.

We were always very surprised to see that -- like you say -- you think that Basie is being shy, you think that Basie is being a very modest guy, making out he's not equipped and this and that. But, drummers today -- there are some good drummers, and some bad ones. As far as playing with the band is concerned, we've got some good drummers. We've had some good drummers in there. And, you know what I mean, and forget where you just left, you see.

they want an act, a show.

You see, and I think the drummer should realize this fact, and you know, like, throw the public -- throw them out of your mind. You know, I mean, get the job done while you're up there, you see.
Yeah. To be there for what you're there for.
Right. For what you're there for. I mean, you look out and see the audience and-- how are they going to concentrate on
what's going on up here if they're up there looking out -- "Everybody's watching me" -- you know.
Yeah.
You know -- and forgetting about the work at hand.

time as the saxophones. So, I mean, you've got to argue all that out.

Right. Yeah. It's alright if they jump (laugh) and then jump back.
Yeah.
You know what I mean. That's really not alright, but, if they're able to jump out there and then come on back --
In other words, to correct their error.

Well, Freddie, so, I mean, now when there's a little conflict like this, now -- then does Basie put his eye on the drummer?

(laugh) I think so. I think he'll either open an eye or something like that. Look at him, and then he'll probably realize what's going on.

See? That's just the same as Ellington, you know?

I mean, it's amazing. There's a second sense, isn't there?

Yeah. Well, you know, Duke was criticized often because some of the things over the years -- the tempo went up, you know -- where he was playing it at what we would say was a bad tempo. Over a period of years it got faster and faster. And one of those was a thing he called 'Ke Ke' -- and critics were very severe about this because he played it faster. It could?

It's not what belongs.
Like, in the beginning, you know, like when you first start something out --
Well, it doesn't swing as much.

No. You see, to me -- you can get so much out of it. I don't know whether they realize that or not. Don't try to get someplace else with it. You see, they're always trying to move ahead. You know, what's the sense of playing if you -- you know -- if you don't play it and enjoy it where it is? Instead of moving on -- trying to, you know, you play like you're trying to get it over with. You see?
Yeah. Distorted?
Yeah.
You mean sort of pushing?
Yeah. Pushing it so you can get it -- it makes it sound like you don't want to tolerate it. You want to get it over with, you know what I mean?
In other words, you're not talking of rushing the tempo, you mean you -- yeah. I can understand that.
You see what I mean? Playing it -- and if you stomp it off in one tempo -- okay -- play it in that tempo and enjoy it right there, you see?

But, some of this is what we talked about before where when you were playing for people dancing -- that whole thing. And, when you're playing for people in a concert hall it's something else. I mean, you know that thing that you played for -- I don't know whether you still play it, but I always hated it from the first --
- Which one?
"Blee Blop Blues".
"Blee Blop Blues". (laugh)
(laugh) I always hated that fast number thing, you know, because everything was rotten on it -- you know -- the tempo, and everything.
You know, I've been trying to remember that tune because I heard it the other day, and I wished I could think of the name, and you just brought it up.
Yeah, but you know --
Yeah, I know. It goes beep beep beep, beep beep beep, beep beep beep.
Yeah. But, you play it in a concert hall and you get a great reaction.
Yes.
But, if you were playing that for anybody to dance to.
No, no. It's not really a dance thing. Unless you're playing for the Lindy Hoppers.
No. I don't think they'd like it.
(laugh)
(laugh) Because they like those fast things like "Jumpin' At The Woodside".
Yeah, but it isn't that it's fast, it's the whole nature combination of the thing.
No, it's the figurations, and, you know -- the figures that --
Yeah. Yeah.
And, it's kind of hard on your trumpets, too.
It's alot of -- you know -- it's alot of noise
about nothing.
Yeah. It is. (laugh) But, it's like a show-stopper as far as the public is concerned, so that's why we do it.
Yeah. Well, it's the old flagwaver.
We were very pleased, Freddie -- well, you were sick. You'd come home. But, we caught the band at Sarasota. And, there was no singer, was there?
No.
And, he played the two He had an intermission, didn't he?
Yeah.
And, it was great, you know, he didn't have -- it wasn't a big -- lots of commercial things, or anything. It was really very good. No singer.
Mm hmm.
We were surprised. It was very nice.

Well, (laugh) as I say -- Joe Williams, you know, like, if it's not Joe Williams, the public would rather not have anybody at all. It would take away -- if it's not Joe Williams, it would take away from them -- you know, --
Right. From the band itself. That's right.
Are you going out to Omaha?
No. I don't think so.
Well, if you go, Preston Love told me that they have a singer there called Walter Devereaux.
Walter Devereaux?
Yeah, and he plays guitar. And, he's a blues singer. And, he's Wynonie Harris's illegitimate son.
Oh, yeah?
And, Preston says he's very good.
Oh, really?
Now, that might be worth looking into.
Okay.
You know, because he's a young, good-looking fellow.
Right. Right. I'll look into that.
I don't know why Preston hasn't spoken to Basie about it. He claims he's very good.
Oh, yeah? I don't know whether we're going to -- I guess we'll probably -- on our way back -- maybe coming back from the coast -- the west coast -- we'll probably stop in there.

Well, let's just speak of the fact -- let's talk about -- we were really speaking about how around the present band -- what changes there were that brought about this present band. I asked when Jimmy Ferrest joined the band, and you said about four years ago.
Mm hmm.
And, Butch came into the band about, like, two and a half years ago.
Two and a half years ago.
These changes have been kind of gradual. I mean, it hasn't been a big upset in the band?
No. No. The changes have been gradual.
When Marshall left the band, that must have been a
change to the band, wasn't it?
It was a change, yeah, because we missed him.
Yeah.
We missed him.
Did Bobby Plater become Straw Koss?
Yeah. Bobby came in, and he took over, and handled it well.
And, handled it well?
Yeah. But, you know, all in all, down through the years, more or less, the band is basically the same, you know.
The way it's been?
The way -- yeah. It's basically the same. But, I would say that it was good, and it's still good. And, you know, down through the years, with all the changes one way or the other ---
It still maintains its character
-- it's still holding up -- you know.

Yeah, but one thing that seems to me different as compared to the old band is that today the soloists are not as important as they used to be. I mean I think what really scores more today are those ensembles.

Well, the ensembles are a headline as far as the band is today, like years ago it used to be the soloists. But, the band -- the present band now don't really rely too much on the soloists. You're right.
There's no soloist of the stature of Lester Young, or---?

Well, no -- it's a different style altogether. And, the feeling is different as far as the playing is concerned. But, where Jimmy Forrest is concerned, he's making a name for himself now, you know, and Eric Dixon has been tremendous, and as a whole, the whole thing is just about terrific as far as I'm concerned now.

Do you think to some extent though, that Basie over the years has learned to be a little, perhaps, distrustful of prima donnas? That he might not want to have too many big stars (laugh) to give him a headache?
I don't know. I don't know how to -- whether --
You must have had enough experience on it.
Yeah. I don't know whether that is true, or not. Or how he feels about it, you know. His reason for not having big name -- big stars.
The payroll must be a very serious factor at all times today, mustn't it? I mean, how you pay this transportation -- you've got one-nighters, and will that pay off?
Well, I don't know too much about that part of it, Stan. You know, I really don't understand what goes on, you know, as far as the payroll is concerned.
But, you know, for years now all the big bands have been doing one-nighters.
Oh, yeah.
Well, we know that that's very expensive to do, because of transportation.

Well, we do alot of concerts now, you see? We're doing alot of concerts, plus, you know, like, high schools, and colleges, you know, and alot of festivals. And, I think that kind of keeps things going.

Freddie, listen, does it ever -- I mean the fact that the gigs now -- they're all involved with a 45 minute performance, and an intermission, and then another 45 minute performance -- which is absolutely nothing like what it once was to play in a band. And, you know, your repertoire is limited and everything -- do you think anybody minds anymore or do you think everybody's just so content to not work too hard, and too long, and get your money just the same, or do you think there's ever times when the guys themselves would like to stretch out?
I think so.
You do?
I do. I think the guys would like to stretch out a little more, because, you know, some of the guys usually go to jam sessions, like, afterwards, if they can find a place to go.
They still do?
Yeah. If they can find a place to go.
But, they can't find them too easily?
Yeah. It's hard to find a place. You can't find it like years ago, you know?
I mean, it's a shame, because, I mean that's the thing about a band, as you said to us before. I mean, you're playing, and, I mean, in the days when people played dances, and you played a set,

it might have been very nice and fine. But, then you play the next set, and for no reason everything is jumping. Everything's terrific, and everybody's really enjoying it. And, if you don't have about seven or eight sets to play a night, or six or something, this can't happen. You've just got two set sets. And, you can't expect anything to happen except what you -- what's supposed to happen.
Yeah. Right. Well, it's a contract thing, you know. That's what I's called. But, we usually play encores, you see?
Yeah. That's right.

We've been doing that quite a bit. Like, we play our regular time, and the public wants more, and so we give them more, you know. We play another number, or -- and if they're not pleased, you know -- if they want more, we give them another number, and then we play the theme song. We usually add two numbers, you know, to the regular format.
Yeah.

When you played this concert you had in Sarasota, now that went -- the playing time must have been over two hours. And, as Helen said, no singer. And, not a very long drum solo. And, everybody in that band got to be featured, you know. It was a very good concert.
Mm hmm.
It was a very nice concert.
Oh, yeah?
And, the audience down there -- the average age was over fifty, but they ate it up.
Oh, yeah. Well, we've been doing that quite a bit. You know, like, our audiences, like, as a rule are like, over fifty, but I've noticed there's alot of kids. Alot of kids are really, you know --
Well, it isn't that it's a young looking band.
Mm hmm. That's what I'm saying, you know what I mean? And, it really make us feel good, you know, that these kids, you know -- coming around, you know?
Yeah. So they're hearing what's you're laying down.
Yeah. They're hearing what's -- right. Because it's all new to them, you know. And, it's really a great thing to --.
Especially for them to hear blues and things that they really don't get to hear anywhere else, do they?
Right. Right. I know. No.
But, it's served up with a -- Basie serves it up with a flair and everything, so that the kids can dig on it.
Yeah.
Well, listen, Freddie, this was a big jolt to everybody when Basie had his attack.
Yes. It was.
Was anybody thinking or worrying, I mean, had he felt bad or anything, or was it totally sudden?

I don't know. I was in the hotel -- the same hotel he was in, and I didn't know anything until the next morning, and he was, like, -- right across -- a couple of doors away from me, you know. He had to walk up some steps to come to his room, see? We both had. So, I didn't know anything until the next morning. I came out, you know, and the guys were standing outside. So, I walked over and said, you know -- "What's happening? Good morning." -- and what not. He said -- "Don't you know? Basie had a heart-attack." And, then naturally I'm upset, you know. So, we didn't know what to do, you know? We knew we had engagements to fill and we thought right away of Nat Pierce and, it really shook everybody up, but we had to, you know, carry on. And, we -- I think we left him there. We had to go out of town -- you know, for some of the engagements, and what-not, and it was really something. The public, you know, they had heard about it, you know, on the television, and what-not. So, as I say, it shook everybody up, you know, but they knew what was happening. The audience -- they went along with us [—].
Yeah. They went along with it very well, didn't they?
Yes, they did.
Because that went on two or three months, didn't it?
Yeah. About -- almost three months, I think.
Yeah. At least.
At least three months.
But, since then he does -- he takes time off occasionally?
Oh, yeah. We take two weeks, three weeks.
How often?
Let's see. I'll say every two months, or maybe every month we'll take a couple of weeks off.
Really?
Yeah.
And, that's primarily to rest him up?
Yes, you know. And, I don't mind it myself, you know, after forty years. (laugh)
(laugh) That gives you more time to play golf?
Right. I'm out on the golf course.
How often did you play?
How often did I play?
Yeah. How often do you play when you're laying off like that?
Well, I'll say, maybe three or four times in a week, you know.
A week? Oh, yeah?
Who do you play with?
Anybody. (laugh) I go to the golf course -- you know, I don't really wait for anybody to go. I just go out there, because you can always get a game out there at the golf course.
But, it's crowded around here.
Around here? Well, I can jump right on the subway and ride to the last stop, and there's a golf course right there, you know.
Where is that?
It's Golf Course. It's at the end of Jerome Avenue subway line.
In the Bronx?
In the Bronx. Yeah. It's easy for me. I could go someplace else, but that's closer.
Yeah. Just take the subway.
All I have to do is walk across the bridge. From where I live it's about, maybe, four or five blocks, and catch the subway and ride to the last stop.
Do you ever play with Budd Johnson?
Years ago I played with Budd. But, I usually -- when I'm in California, I usually play with Joe Williams,
Oh, you do.
It's Charles Thompson who's practically a professional, isn't he?
Yeah. That's what everybody tells me. I haven't, you know -- it's been ages.
Did you ever play with him?
I played with him -- what -- maybe ten years ago. And, he was good then, and I've heard that he's supposedly a professional now. I don't know.
I think he tricks people.
Oh, yeah?
I think he lets them think he's just a piano player, and then they get a bet.
(laugh) No. I haven't run into him lately on the golf course.
But, that's one way you have of keeping fit?
Yeah. I usually go out and play. I love the game.
Do you take your clubs on the road at all?
Whenever I'm going on location, or whatever part of it that we come to that the sun is shining, or time of year that we go, or if we go to California, I take them with me.
Are there any other guys in the band that like to play?
Bobby Plater.
Bobby plays. He's about the only one.
He's about the only one?
Bobby's another quiet guy.
Yes.
I wish he'd take more solos. I like the way he plays.
Yes. He plays beautifully.
You know, when he -- I mean apart from those ballads, when he --
Well, no. He can swing too.
Yeah. He can sound a bit like Benny Carter.
Right. And, he should. He really should.
The other guy's quite nice, too. What's his name? The other alto?
Danny?
Yeah.
Danny Turner? You like him?
Yeah.
Yeah.
I think he's a little more --
Modern, yeah.
-- beboppish but still good.
Yeah. Yeah.
In fact, that's a good sax section.
Yeah. He's technical.
He's what?
Technical.
Technical.
Yes. But, still he's got some imagination.
Oh, yes.
Yeah. It's very technical.
Yes.
Do you still have to play the peace-maker at any time, in the bus, or anything, or occasionally? Is that a role for you anymore?
Not really.
No?
No.
Maybe guys don't feel so serious about things, or anything.
Not really. Not like back in the days --

segments.title: Birth in Charleston and Dafts Court
segments.summary: Greene gives his birth date and describes the court off Rutledge Avenue where he was born and lived until 1923.

segments.title: His brothers Clarence and Josey
segments.summary: He names his two younger brothers and says neither was musical; one works as a cook at the Charleston Navy Yard.

segments.title: His father's harmonium and early death
segments.summary: His father played a foot organ at an aunt's house; he cannot recall the repertoire and says his father died when he was about ten or eleven.

segments.title: His mother raising the boys alone
segments.summary: After his father's death his mother did domestic work, and he was often home from school before she was.

segments.title: Boyhood mischief and conditions in Charleston
segments.summary: He recalls court friends, selling papers and shining shoes, and the racial problems and poverty of Charleston.

segments.title: Leaving Charleston for New York in 1923
segments.summary: He explains that he went north at twelve or thirteen, travelling by train with his uncle's wife to his mother's sister.

segments.title: Burying his mother and marrying in Charleston
segments.summary: Flashing forward, he says he went back when his mother died at eighteen or nineteen, and married there.

segments.title: A part of the gang, playing ball
segments.summary: Asked about his character as a child, he says he went along with the group and played sports, a skinny kid.

segments.title: Church singing, the ukulele and street-corner quartets
segments.summary: His mother sang in the AME choir; he played ukulele and sang baritone in a street-corner quartet.

segments.title: Dancing and stage shows in Charleston theaters
segments.summary: He loved dancing and the movie houses with stage shows, sat in the balcony, and imitated the dancers at home.

segments.title: The Whitman Sisters, Pops and Louie and Mamie Smith
segments.summary: He recalls the Whitman Sisters and their young dancer and a visit by Mamie Smith, with a small group behind her.

segments.title: Jenkins' Orphanage bands
segments.summary: He describes the orphanage's five or six brass bands, which played on street corners to raise money, and names Charlie Anderson and others who came from it.

segments.title: Child musicians on the corners and Greene following the bands
segments.summary: The boys played from about seven to fifteen across the whole city, and hearing the brass is what drew Greene to music.

segments.title: Reverend Jenkins and life in the orphanage
segments.summary: He describes the director, the big stone building, and Cat Anderson's report of severe punishments.

segments.title: Closeness to his mother and friends leaving for the North
segments.summary: He recaps his musical beginnings, says he was close to his mother, and describes his gang moving north.

segments.title: His stepfather and his mother's baking
segments.summary: He says his half-brothers had a different father, that the stepfather was a contractor, and that his mother was a fine baker.

segments.title: Theater glamour and his mother's secret marriage
segments.summary: He liked everything about the theaters; Helen and Stanley Dance say his mother may have married in secret to settle him down.

segments.title: Arriving at his aunt's apartment in the Sixties
segments.summary: He describes his aunt's rooms off the West Sixties and who stayed with them.

segments.title: Musicians around the neighborhood: Benny Carter, Freddie Jenkins
segments.summary: He did not know Benny Carter then, but recalls Freddie Jenkins living nearby and a mystery musician in a big car.

segments.title: PS 58 and Hell's Kitchen gangs
segments.summary: He names his public school and says he remembers nothing of Irish gangs or kids running drugs.

segments.title: The Charleston dance craze and a gang leader friend
segments.summary: After knocking down the neighborhood tough he became friends and danced the Charleston with him on corners.

segments.title: His Charleston sweetheart Leotha
segments.summary: He tells of the girl in the court who became his wife and greeted him when he returned to bury his mother.

segments.title: Moving to Harlem and changing schools
segments.summary: His aunt moved to West 131st Street, near the Lafayette Theater and the Rhythm Club, which meant a new school and gang.

segments.title: Hell's Kitchen migration and Harlem jumping
segments.summary: He agrees people drifted out of Hell's Kitchen and that Harlem was where things were happening when he was about fifteen.

segments.title: PS 5 and living with his aunt
segments.summary: He recalls the school at 141st Street and the several apartments they moved between, with his aunt as a foster mother.

segments.title: Junior high and working after school
segments.summary: He left Frederick Douglass junior high after a couple of years to work, and shoveled snow for money.

segments.title: Living in the Lafayette and Lincoln theaters
segments.summary: He spent his time at the Lafayette and Lincoln theaters, paid for by his aunt or friends.

segments.title: Victrola records and first impressions of Duke and Fletcher
segments.summary: He recalls a grand-aunt's Victrola and thinks he heard Ellington, McKinney's and perhaps Fletcher Henderson, with Stanley Dance sorting out the dates.

segments.title: No phonograph at home, the theaters as his school
segments.summary: Without records at home, the stage shows were his main source of music, more than the movies.

segments.title: The Renaissance ballroom, Vernon Andrade and the 101 Ranch
segments.summary: He recalls going to the Renaissance, where Vernon Andrade was house band, and the 101 Ranch, and sorts out timing.

segments.title: House rent parties and the stride pianist Rock
segments.summary: His aunt gave rent parties with a hired stride pianist called Rock, and young Freddie moved the furniture.

segments.title: Picking up banjo and guitar; the Yeah Man Club
segments.summary: He moved from ukulele to banjo and then guitar, and mentions his first job at the Yeah Man before reordering his story.

segments.title: The Rhythm Club corner: Jelly Roll Morton and Chick Webb
segments.summary: As a student he passed the Rhythm Club, remembering Jelly Roll saying he taught everyone to swing.

segments.title: Choosing music; marrying Leotha Elmo
segments.summary: He says music made him happiest after other jobs and names his wife Leotha Elmo.

segments.title: Learning scales with a trumpet-playing friend
segments.summary: In Charleston he studied scales on a blackboard at the home of trumpeter Samuel Walker, whose father taught at Jenkins'.

segments.title: Dart's Hall and the visiting big bands
segments.summary: Bands such as Belton's and the Golden Pheasant played Dart's Hall; banjo and tuba carried the sound before microphones.

segments.title: Sitting in with the Nighthawks on a pawn-shop banjo
segments.summary: He bought a banjo in a pawn shop and talked his way into rehearsals with the Nighthawks, his first professional work.

segments.title: Professor Blake's library at Jenkins'
segments.summary: A brass teacher from Jenkins' who had studied at Howard let him use his music books on Sundays.

segments.title: A year in Charleston; his son is born
segments.summary: He stayed a year or more, helped his father-in-law the contractor, and his first son was born.

segments.title: Touring Maine with the Jenkins' Orphanage band
segments.summary: He left with the orphanage show touring Maine in a homemade bus, playing Grange halls in uniform.

segments.title: Leotha's reaction and why he had to leave Charleston
segments.summary: He explains that he knew music had to come from New York, though his wife did not want him to go.

segments.title: Staying in New York and sending for his family
segments.summary: After Maine he stayed in New York, sent for his wife and child, and worked as an upholsterer by day.

segments.chapter: Uptown clubs and the Black Cat
segments.title: Lonnie Simmons gets him the Yeah Man job
segments.summary: His school friend Lonnie Simmons, a tenor man from Mount Pleasant, got him the job in a trio with pianist Eric Henry.

segments.chapter: Uptown clubs and the Black Cat
segments.title: Switching from banjo to guitar
segments.summary: The club manager told him to get a guitar, which he bought on time at King's on 47th Street.

segments.chapter: Uptown clubs and the Black Cat
segments.title: Celebrities in the after-hours at the Yeah Man
segments.summary: Lonnie Johnson, Jimmy Dorsey, June Clark and others dropped in, and Greene and Simmons were awestruck country boys.

segments.chapter: Uptown clubs and the Black Cat
segments.title: What became of Lonnie Simmons
segments.summary: Simmons went to Chicago, worked at the Club De Lisa, and switched to organ.

segments.chapter: Uptown clubs and the Black Cat
segments.title: The Exclusive Club and working with Willie Gant
segments.summary: He moved with Simmons to the Exclusive Club and played in a duo with stride pianist Willie Gant.

segments.chapter: Uptown clubs and the Black Cat
segments.title: Willie Gant as mentor
segments.summary: Greene says Gant was much older, kind, and gave him an education in accompanying singers.

segments.chapter: Uptown clubs and the Black Cat
segments.title: Gant's repertoire and accompanying Amanda Randolph
segments.summary: Gant played all the popular songs, accompanied Amanda Randolph, and could stride.

segments.chapter: Uptown clubs and the Black Cat
segments.title: Luckey Roberts and records with James P.
segments.summary: Greene never heard Luckey Roberts, and mentions making records with James P. Johnson and Pee Wee Russell.

segments.chapter: Uptown clubs and the Black Cat
segments.title: The Exclusive Club crowd and playing without a drummer
segments.summary: Celebrities came less often than at the Yeah Man; he handled tempo for dancers and acted as the drummer.

segments.chapter: Uptown clubs and the Black Cat
segments.title: Guitar or bass with piano; doubts about soloing
segments.summary: Helen and Stanley Dance discuss piano-bass duos and cabaret licenses; Greene says he was not ready to solo then.

segments.chapter: Uptown clubs and the Black Cat
segments.title: The Black Cat in the Village with Kenny Clarke
segments.summary: He and Lonnie Simmons joined a rhythm section at the Black Cat with Kenny Clarke, Fat Atkins and Frank Spearman.

segments.chapter: Uptown clubs and the Black Cat
segments.title: Black Cat hours, John Hammond and the audition
segments.summary: They played midnight to four; Hammond heard him there and set up the audition at the Roseland for Basie.

segments.title: The party at Mills and the jam session
segments.summary: Greene and the Danses recall Helen Dance's party, his first jam session, where everyone was present.

segments.title: The party as publicity and who was there
segments.summary: Stanley Dance calls it a publicity stunt; they list guests and agree the Basie men were the thrill.

segments.title: Basie's New York arrival and the Roseland opening
segments.summary: They discuss Hammond polishing the band, additions to the Kansas City group, and a rough opening night.

segments.title: The audition with the Basie band
segments.summary: He describes walking in scared, playing the blues, Basie's silence, and being told to work that night.

segments.title: First recording date with Billie Holiday and Lester Young
segments.summary: Days later he arrived first at the studio and recorded with Billie, Teddy Wilson, Lester, Buck Clayton and Jo Jones.

segments.title: Cat Anderson and the Maine tour band
segments.summary: After a tape change, Greene explains Cat Anderson and Julius Walker were in the Jenkins' band that went to Maine.

segments.title: After the session; Lester Young's sound
segments.summary: He describes the quiet elevator ride and how Lester's sound differed from Coleman Hawkins and other New York tenors.

segments.title: Joining the band in Pittsburgh
segments.summary: He recalls the William Penn Hotel as his first job with Basie and cannot recall how he got there.

segments.title: Bobby Moore and the 1937 trumpet personnel
segments.summary: With the discography, they sort out the trumpet and reed changes in the band in March to June 1937.

segments.title: First night: single-string versus playing rhythm
segments.summary: He felt like a stranger, tried single-string playing, and was told to keep time; he has played rhythm since.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: Staying out of the way of Basie, Jo Jones and Walter Page
segments.summary: He explains how the three traded phrases and broke the rhythm while he kept time steady.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: Walter Page
segments.summary: Greene describes Page as a good timekeeper who gave breaks and held things together, and was well trained.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: The rhythm section as the band's engine; Basie sets tempos
segments.summary: Helen Dance asks about the roles of the four; Greene says Basie set all tempos and the rest understood each other.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: Jo Jones's personality and other great drummers
segments.summary: They discuss controlling Jo, whom Greene says has not changed, and compare Alvin Burroughs and Shadow Wilson.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: Feeling at home in the rhythm section; the All American Rhythm Section
segments.summary: It took him a while to feel he belonged; he took his cue from Basie and enjoyed the rhythm-section records.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: The band as a happy family
segments.summary: The band got along despite varied personalities and had a ball.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: Lester Young and Herschel Evans: two camps of fans
segments.summary: Greene says each tenor had his fans but he never saw bad feeling between them.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: Lester Young the person and the stylist
segments.summary: They discuss Lester's private world, his melodic, swinging playing, and that he never fully matured.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: How much did Lester shape the Basie sound?
segments.summary: Stanley Dance argues the Moten band already had the Basie principles, while Helen Dance stresses Lester.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: The peak period of the band
segments.summary: Asked directly, Greene says he loved playing behind Lester and that the early years were the greatest.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: A looser band, with head arrangements
segments.summary: The early band was relaxed and free, with many head arrangements and riffs worked up in the band.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: Lester Young's humor and life on the bus
segments.summary: Lester was the funniest man in the band, calling men 'lady' and keeping the bus laughing; Basie rode with them.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: Greene as the peacemaker
segments.summary: He says he was always the peacemaker among the men who went out together.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: How new men fit in; Basie controls with a look
segments.summary: New players such as Sweets Edison fit in; Basie keeps order without words.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: Great bands as families: the Lunceford band
segments.summary: They compare Basie with Jimmie Lunceford's band, which Greene first saw at the Lafayette with Curtis Simmons.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: Basie's secret: he wants to be sent
segments.summary: The Danses and Greene reflect on Basie's gift as rhythmic and on how simple his leadership is.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: Personalities: Buck Clayton, Jack Washington and Herschel Evans
segments.summary: They discuss Buck, the quiet Jack Washington, and Herschel's insistence that Greene play rhythm.

segments.chapter: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
segments.title: Who Greene hung out with; Basie on the road
segments.summary: He roomed with Buck, Lester and Sweets, and Basie often joined them; Lester went out jamming.

segments.title: Jimmy Rushing
segments.summary: Greene recalls Rushing as a funny storyteller, light on his feet, and his struggles with weight.

segments.title: Wives on the road
segments.summary: Musicians brought wives only for long engagements; Greene knew of no band-wife problems.

segments.title: John Hammond and Basie's way of saying yes
segments.summary: Helen Dance suggests Hammond tried to steer Basie; Greene says he saw nothing of it.

segments.title: 'St. Louis Blues' and Basie dealing with advisers
segments.summary: Stanley Dance recalls Basie calling an arrangement a satire to Teddy Reig; Greene says he doesn't interfere.

segments.title: Bad nights and Basie's calm
segments.summary: Greene says he used to be upset when the rhythm was off but now takes it in stride; Basie stays calm.

segments.title: The first departures: Herschel Evans, Walter Page and the trombones
segments.summary: They recall Herschel going first and Buddy Tate replacing him, and trombone changes through 1939.

segments.title: Billie Holiday with the band
segments.summary: Billie's stint was short; Helen Dance says Billie told her Freddie was the only man she really loved.

segments.title: Helen Humes
segments.summary: Greene liked Helen Humes as a good band singer who fit the band.

segments.title: Hiring and firing
segments.summary: Greene says he stays away from who is hired and fired.

segments.title: Jo Jones and Lester Young drafted
segments.summary: They recall that Jo and Lester went into the Army, which hurt the band; Shadow Wilson took over.

segments.title: The 1944-45 band line-up
segments.summary: Stanley Dance reads off personnel, with Greene recalling nicknames like Mutton-Leg.

segments.title: Lucky Thompson in the band
segments.summary: Greene says Lucky sounded very good in the band and recalls that few stayed long.

segments.title: Earl Warren's absence and the new trumpets
segments.summary: They trace Earl Warren, Snooky Young, J. J. Johnson and others, and wonder when the draft ended.

segments.title: The 1946 line-up with Paul Gonsalves
segments.summary: With Jo and Walter back, Dance reads the band; Greene says Gonsalves worked out beautifully.

segments.title: Preston Love and C. Q. Price
segments.summary: Greene says Preston idolized Earl Warren and that C. Q. Price was a third alto from Buffalo.

segments.title: Wartime travel and the reunion of 1946
segments.summary: They discuss buses and trains in wartime and how good it was to have Jo and Walter back.

segments.title: Don Byas, Paul Bascomb and Tab Smith
segments.summary: They try to place Don Byas and Paul Bascomb in the 1940-42 band.

segments.title: When Lester left and whether he returned
segments.summary: They sort out dates for Lester's leaving, the Kansas City Five records and his Army service.

segments.title: The late-1940s band; Jo leaves, Shadow Wilson falls ill
segments.summary: Dance reads personnel for 1947-49; Greene recalls Butch Ballard and Shadow's illness.

segments.title: Why the band changed: bebop and the closing ballrooms
segments.summary: They conclude it was a transition, with bebop, better-paid sidemen, and ballrooms closing.

segments.chapter: Small group, new sound and Europe
segments.title: Let go for two months and working with Lester Young at Birdland
segments.summary: When Basie cut down to a small group Greene was let go for two months, worked with Lester, then was recalled.

segments.chapter: Small group, new sound and Europe
segments.title: The 1950-51 small group's personnel
segments.summary: They sort out members of the small group, including Clark Terry, Wardell Gray and Marshall Royal.

segments.chapter: Small group, new sound and Europe
segments.title: How the small group went over
segments.summary: It lasted about two years, played small clubs and Canada, and the public did not take to it much.

segments.chapter: Small group, new sound and Europe
segments.title: Marshall Royal and discipline in the rebuilt band
segments.summary: Greene agrees the band of 1952 had a different character, with Marshall Royal as bandmaster.

segments.chapter: Small group, new sound and Europe
segments.title: Neal Hefti and The Atomic Basie
segments.summary: They discuss Hefti's arrangements as a formula that arrangers imitated.

segments.chapter: Small group, new sound and Europe
segments.title: The 1952-53 line-ups; Frank Foster and Ernie Wilkins
segments.summary: Dance reads personnel; Greene says Foster and Wilkins were a new phase.

segments.chapter: Small group, new sound and Europe
segments.title: First European tour
segments.summary: He describes the thrill of the 1954 trip, the reception, and the 1957 Royal Command Performance.

segments.chapter: Small group, new sound and Europe
segments.title: Basie's stage presence and television manner
segments.summary: They say Basie is natural on television and that he says little.

segments.chapter: Small group, new sound and Europe
segments.title: Joe Williams and 'Every Day'
segments.summary: Greene recalls Joe Williams as an usher he'd forgotten and how the hit saved the band.

segments.chapter: Small group, new sound and Europe
segments.title: Foster, Wess and the band's 1950s success
segments.summary: The writing and flute work of Foster and Wess kept the band going and growing.

segments.chapter: Small group, new sound and Europe
segments.title: Arrangers from inside the band versus outsiders
segments.summary: Stanley Dance asks why outside arrangers are hired; Greene does not know the money.

segments.chapter: Small group, new sound and Europe
segments.title: A family again, and long stays at Birdland
segments.summary: After Foster and Wess the band got back into a family groove, with long Birdland stays.

segments.chapter: Small group, new sound and Europe
segments.title: Backing Sinatra and Tony Bennett
segments.summary: They discuss recordings and appearances with Sinatra, Bennett and Ella, and the Sands in Las Vegas.

segments.title: Basie's stagecraft compared with Ellington on television
segments.summary: Greene says Basie had been on stage long before the band and his shyness is part of his act.

segments.title: Drummers should keep the tempo, not play to the public
segments.summary: Greene says the rhythm should follow Basie's tempo start to finish and that the public ruins drummers by wanting a show.

segments.title: Drummers supporting soloists and jumping the gun
segments.summary: Greene says drummers should back the soloist, accent brass figures on time, and not rush ahead of the beat.

segments.title: How Basie sets the tempo and why tempos creep up
segments.summary: Greene says Basie sets tempo by the audience; today many pieces are played too fast.

segments.title: 'Blee Blop Blues' and concert versus dance music
segments.summary: They talk of a fast show-stopper that works in concert halls but not for dancing.

segments.title: No singer at Sarasota; Joe Williams still the standard
segments.summary: Greene says the public wants Joe Williams or no singer; Dance suggests Walter Devereaux of Omaha.

segments.title: Gradual changes to the present band
segments.summary: New players like Jimmy Forrest and Butch Miles came gradually, and the loss of Marshall Royal was felt.

segments.title: No big stars, payroll and one-nighters
segments.summary: Greene says ensembles now outweigh soloists, and concerts, schools and festivals keep the band working.

segments.title: Short sets, encores and the audience
segments.summary: Greene says the men would like to stretch out and that audiences are mostly over fifty.

segments.title: Basie's heart attack
segments.summary: He tells how he learned the morning after, how the band carried on, and the break lasting almost three months.

segments.title: Golf
segments.summary: He plays golf three or four times a week in the Bronx and carries his clubs on the road.

segments.title: Bobby Plater and Danny Turner in the sax section
segments.summary: They praise Plater and Turner; at the close Greene says he no longer has to play peacemaker.
